projects.title: DEMI — Digital twin of smart buildings
projects.summary: A complete digital twin of smart campus buildings, with live dashboards and a natural-language assistant powered by local AI.

problem: Smart buildings now combine many energy systems: EV chargers, solar panels, batteries and the building's own consumption. Each one produces its own data, in its own format, on its own platform. For the people running the campus, there was no single place to see what was happening, no way to test a decision before applying it, and no way to ask a simple question without writing database queries.
The goal of DEMI was to build a digital twin: a live, faithful software copy of these buildings that gathers all their data, shows it clearly, and lets operators interact with it in plain language.
stateOfArt: Digital twins are common in industry and energy, but they are usually built on closed, proprietary platforms. In smart cities, the open FIWARE ecosystem and the NGSI-LD standard offer a shared way to describe and exchange data about connected devices, which makes them a natural foundation for an open, interoperable twin.

On the AI side, recent research shows that large language models can turn natural-language questions into database queries and help understand what an operator actually wants, but most of this work relies on cloud models. Running the models locally keeps the infrastructure's data on site. DEMI started from an earlier FIWARE prototype from the lab, which provided an initial data model and setup.
contribution: Led the design and development end to end, turning the initial prototype into a complete platform.
Extended the NGSI-LD data model with new entities for solar panels, batteries and buildings, so the twin covers the whole energy system and not only the chargers.
Built the data pipelines that bring years of real charging and energy data into the twin, through the FIWARE context broker and a time-series database, with checks that every update arrives intact.

Designed and built the interactive dashboard from scratch: campus map, energy flows, charging timelines per port, monthly and hourly analyses, and a switch between historical data and live digital-twin data.
Built Pipeline Check, a sandboxed tool where anyone can change any value in the twin and watch it travel through the whole system, without touching real data.
Integrated local AI: an assistant that turns plain-English questions into database queries and explains the answer, with a benchmark of generated questions used to measure and improve its accuracy.

Built a live control service where operators give commands in plain language, and a monitoring page where the site reacts to "what if" scenarios (grid limits, less sun, every charger busy), followed by an AI-written summary of what happened.
Made the whole stack reproducible: containerised with Docker, with scripts that install, start and reset everything on a new machine.

technologies.v: FIWARE Orion-LD, QuantumLeap, NGSI-LD, CrateDB, MongoDB
Local large language models (Ollama), natural-language-to-SQL, FastAPI
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet maps, Chart.js
Docker, Docker Compose, Jupyter notebooks, shell scripts

outcome: DEMI became a working digital twin of the campus buildings: real data flows into it, it can be explored visually or questioned in plain English, and scenarios can be simulated before acting on the real site. Everything runs on local machines, with no data sent to external AI services.

The project also documents its limits openly, such as gaps between data sources and the speed of local AI without a dedicated graphics card, and lays the groundwork for a future charging-coordination algorithm.

projects.title: Code Generation Crew
projects.summary: AI agents on local models that write, review and test code together in a closed feedback loop until the program works.

problem: A single AI model asked to write code often produces something that looks right but does not run, misses edge cases, or quietly answers a different question. The problem gets worse with small models that run on a personal computer: they are private, free and offline, but much less reliable than large cloud models.
The question behind this project: can several small local models, each with one clear job and checking each other's work, produce code that actually works, without sending anything to the cloud?
stateOfArt: Code assistants built on large cloud models have become very capable, but they need an internet connection, an API key, and sending your code to an external service. Research on "self-debugging" and on multi-agent frameworks shows that letting models review, test and correct their own output improves results, since the program can be run and the errors fed back.
Most of that work, however, relies on the largest available models. Much less is known about how far the same ideas can carry small models that fit on a laptop.
contribution: Designed a team of AI agents with separate responsibilities: one turns a vague request into a precise specification, one writes the code, one reviews it without running it, and one writes and runs unit tests.

Built a closed feedback loop: when the review or the tests fail, the exact errors go back to the agent writing the code, which tries again with that context until the program passes, within a configurable number of attempts.
Added automatic test generation, so every program is checked against tests written for that specific request, plus a style check that reports issues without blocking the result.
Ran everything on local models through Ollama, with no API keys and no data leaving the machine, and made it easy to switch between several open models.

Built a desktop application around it: prompt, refined specification and generated code in resizable panels, syntax highlighting, saved sessions with their full history, and one-click opening in VS Code.
Created a benchmark of tasks from easy to very hard, written both as short simple requests and as detailed specifications, to measure how well the system really performs.

technologies.v: LangGraph (multi-agent workflow), LangChain, local LLMs through Ollama
Tkinter desktop app, Pygments syntax highlighting, VS Code integration

outcome: Working together in the loop, small local models produced correct, tested programs on the large majority of the benchmark, including every one of the hardest tasks.

An unexpected finding: the system did better with detailed, precise requests than with short ones. Clear specifications reduce ambiguity and help the agents agree, which is exactly what the specification step is there for.

projects.title: Driver for an undocumented camera
projects.summary: A cheap pan-tilt camera with no usable driver: I mapped how it really moves, then wrote a driver to control it and capture photos and video.

problem: I had a cheap pan-tilt camera, the kind sold to be used only through the manufacturer's phone app. There was no driver to control it from my own programs. A few low-level functions existed, but they were undocumented: I could make the camera move, but not know in which direction, along which axis, or by how much.
The goal was to take full control of the camera from my own code: point it precisely, and take photos or record video exactly when I need to.
stateOfArt: Low-cost Wi-Fi cameras usually work only through their vendor's app and cloud. Standard camera protocols are often missing or only partly supported, and when low-level commands exist they are rarely documented, so open-source tools either do not support these models or only offer basic video viewing.
contribution: Explored the camera's low-level functions and found which ones actually make it move.
Measured its real behaviour by observing it physically: sending commands, watching how the camera actually turned, and recording the results.
Used those measurements to work out what each command really does: which axis it moves, in which direction and by how much.
Wrote a driver on top of this model that moves the camera to where I want it, instead of sending blind commands.
Added photo and video capture on demand, controlled from my own programs.

technologies.v: ESP32 microcontroller, low-cost pan-tilt Wi-Fi camera
Reverse engineering by observation, behaviour measurement and calibration

outcome: A camera that was only usable through its own app can now be controlled precisely from my own code, and takes pictures or videos whenever I ask it to. A personal project, done for the fun of making cheap hardware do things it was never designed for.

projects.title: Linux USB Gadgets
projects.summary: A BeagleBone board that becomes a USB drive, a network card or a touchpad when plugged into a computer.

problem: Small Linux boards such as the BeagleBone Black can do more than act as tiny computers: plugged into a PC over USB, they can pretend to be a USB device, such as a network card, a USB drive or an input device. This "USB gadget" mode is useful for embedded products and test benches.

In practice it is hard to set up. Documentation is scattered, the board keeps falling back to its default network mode, settings disappear after a reboot, and sharing the PC's internet connection with the board breaks easily.
stateOfArt: Linux supports USB gadgets in two ways: older single-purpose modules, each turning the board into one kind of device, and the more recent ConfigFS framework, which lets several functions be combined into one composite device (storage, network, serial and input at once). Most tutorials online cover only one case, are written for older systems, or skip the steps needed to make the setup survive a reboot.
contribution: Set up the board from scratch: flashed a Debian IoT image onto a microSD card and configured it at first boot through a serial console.
Made the board work as a network card over USB, with the PC sharing its internet connection (IP forwarding, NAT with iptables, DNS), and tested connectivity end to end.
Diagnosed and fixed a bug where internet access stopped after installing a desktop environment on the board, then made the fix permanent with a systemd service and persistent firewall rules.
Gave the board a remote graphical desktop through VNC.
Configured the board as a USB drive with ConfigFS, creating a FAT disk image and getting past the board's habit of always presenting itself as a network device.
Programmed the board to appear as an input device such as a touchpad.
Wrote a complete step-by-step guide with ready-to-use scripts, so the whole setup can be reproduced from a blank board.

technologies.v: Debian Linux, Linux USB gadget framework (ConfigFS, libcomposite), systemd
IP forwarding, NAT with iptables, DNS, VNC
Bash, C, Python, serial console (Minicom), balenaEtcher

outcome: The board reliably shows up as the USB device we choose (network card, storage or input device), and the configuration survives reboots. The guide and scripts let the next person go from a blank board to a working setup without repeating the same trial and error.

projects.title: Arduino Music Player
projects.summary: A low-power educational music player with a screen and LEDs that visualise the notes, squeezed into a microcontroller's memory.

problem: Students learning music and students learning programming rarely get a tool that connects the two. Music education often relies on expensive instruments or software, and programming exercises often lack a tangible, creative result you can actually hear and see.
The goal was a small, affordable and low-power device that plays music while showing how it works: which note is playing, at which frequency, and how a microcontroller produces it.
stateOfArt: Phones and MP3 players play music perfectly well, but they hide everything that happens inside. Arduino music projects exist, but most play a single tune and quickly run out of memory: the Arduino Uno has very little RAM, so storing many melodies and driving a screen at the same time is a real constraint.
contribution: Designed the full device around an Arduino Uno: a passive buzzer for precise notes, an OLED screen, a row of LEDs with one LED per note of the scale, and push buttons for play, pause, next, previous and volume.
Wrote the firmware in C/C++ as a non-blocking loop, so the device stays responsive to the buttons while music is playing, with debouncing for reliable presses.

Optimised memory so a whole library of melodies fits: melodies stored in flash memory instead of RAM, compact data structures, only the selected melody loaded, and the screen redrawn only when needed.
Added live memory monitoring to track free RAM and prevent crashes, which made it possible to keep the screen and the full melody library together.
Synchronised the LEDs with the notes, so each note lights its own LED and the melody turns into a light show that shows the scale.
Designed an IoT extension with a WiFi module connected to the Arduino, to download new melodies, share compositions and connect to classroom or smart-home systems.

technologies.v: Arduino Uno, passive buzzer, SSD1306 OLED display (I2C), LEDs, push buttons
Wire (I2C), Adafruit GFX, Adafruit SSD1306, avr/pgmspace (flash storage)

outcome: A working music player, with the complete code and a demo running in the Wokwi simulator: it plays a library of well-known melodies, shows the song and volume on screen and lights the matching LED for every note, while staying within the Arduino's tight memory limits.
Built for an M.Sc. course on sustainable IoT, the project shows how careful memory management makes a very small, low-power board do much more than expected.

projects.title: Business websites
projects.summary: Showcase and sales websites for businesses in equipment sales and repair, AI training and construction services.

problem: Small businesses win most of their clients online: people search for a service in their area, compare a few websites and ask for a quote. Without a clear, credible site that explains their offer and makes it easy to get in touch, they lose those clients to competitors.
Each of the businesses I worked with needed a site that presents a wide range of services clearly, works well on phones, and turns visitors into quote requests.
stateOfArt: Website builders and ready-made themes make it easy to put a page online, but generic templates rarely fit a business with many services, regional coverage or specific requests. Fully custom development, on the other hand, is costly for a small company and hard for it to update. A content management system such as WordPress, carefully structured and configured, sits in between: professional, affordable and easy to keep up to date.
contribution: Built the sites end to end on my own: understanding each business, structuring the content, design, development, hosting and deployment.
An equipment sales, rental and repair company: product and service catalogue, brand-specific repair pages, spare parts, maintenance contracts, training, and quote requests.
An AI training organisation: course catalogues for companies and individuals, course pages, trainer profiles, a blog, regional pages and an interactive online test.
A rope-access building contractor: services organised by type of work, pages for each area served, a project gallery, safety and certification information, and an emergency contact.
Designed every site around clear navigation, mobile-friendly layouts and visible calls to action leading to contact and quote forms.

technologies.v: Hosting, domain and deployment setup, ongoing updates

outcome: The businesses got professional, easy-to-navigate websites that present their whole offer and bring in contact and quote requests, and that they can keep updating themselves. Detailed client names stay private.

projects.title: Email campaign automation
projects.summary: A desktop tool that sends advertising campaigns at a natural pace during business hours, so the emails land in the inbox, not in spam.

problem: A client wanted to reach many professional contacts, such as sports clubs and hotels, with an advertising campaign. Sending that many emails by hand takes days, and sending them all at once from one account is the fastest way to be flagged as spam: messages end up in junk folders or the account gets blocked.
The goal was a tool that sends a personalised campaign automatically, at a pace that looks like normal human activity, so the emails actually reach the inbox.
stateOfArt: Email marketing platforms solve deliverability with dedicated sending infrastructure, but they are paid, require importing the contact list into an external service, and do not send from the company's own mailbox. Simple mail-merge tools send from your own account but fire everything at once, with no control over pace, timing or duplicates.
contribution: Built a desktop application that loads contact lists from Excel files, checks every address and sends a personalised HTML email through the company's own Outlook mailbox.
Made sending look natural: random limits per minute, per hour and per day, pauses between batches, and an adjustable speed cap.
Restricted sending to business hours on working days, with French public holidays calculated automatically, including the movable ones that depend on Easter.
Kept a log of everything sent, tied to each campaign, so a contact never receives the same campaign twice, even after a restart.
Added one-click unsubscribe headers, as mailbox providers expect from legitimate senders.
Added previews and draft creation, so a campaign can be checked before anything is sent, and improved the tool through many successive versions.

technologies.v: Microsoft Outlook automation (win32com), HTML email templates, List-Unsubscribe headers
pandas, Excel contact lists, sent-email log

outcome: The client could run campaigns to large contact lists from their own mailbox without doing anything by hand, with emails sent at a natural pace during working hours and reaching inboxes instead of spam folders. The client's name stays private.

projects.title: Computer-lab management platform
projects.summary: A web platform to share a lab's computers between many users: allocation, monitoring and blocking users, with admin and user roles.

problem: In a university lab, many students and researchers need the same computers at the same times. Without a system, the result is conflicts, machines taken without notice, nobody knowing who used what, and no way for the lab managers to step in when someone misuses the equipment.
The goal of our final-year project was a web platform to organise the lab: who can use which computer and when, with oversight for the people running it.
stateOfArt: Many labs still rely on paper sign-up sheets, shared spreadsheets or messaging groups, which give no real-time view and no control. Generic booking tools exist, but they are not built around shared computers, user accounts with different roles, and the monitoring a lab needs.
contribution: Worked in a team of three, where I led the front end: the interface every user and administrator sees.
Designed and built the main screens: sign-up and login, the dashboard, a calendar for booking computers, notifications, statistics charts, user profiles and a research section.
Built the interface around the allocation system, so users can see which computers are available and book them, and administrators can follow activity and block users when needed.
Handled the different roles in the interface, with administrators and regular users each seeing what they need.
Connected the interface to the platform's PHP back end, built with the Laravel framework.

technologies.v: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React (dashboard), Laravel Blade templates, Vite
Authentication, role-based access, booking calendar, notifications, charts

outcome: A working web platform that lets a lab share its computers between many users in an organised way, with booking, monitoring and administration in one place. It was our B.Sc. final-year project and my first large team project.

projects.title: Markov chain visualiser
projects.summary: Draw a Markov chain and get its matrix, or fill a matrix and get the graph with directed, weighted arrows.

problem: A Markov chain can be written in two ways: as a transition matrix, a table of probabilities, or as a graph of states connected by weighted arrows. Students and teachers constantly switch between the two, and doing it by hand is slow and error-prone, especially drawing the graph cleanly with every arrow, direction and probability in the right place.
The goal was a desktop application that converts automatically in both directions: fill in a matrix and get the graph, or build a graph and get the matrix.
stateOfArt: At the time, the usual options were drawing graphs by hand, general-purpose drawing software, or writing scripts in mathematical tools. None of them offered a simple interface that goes both ways between matrix and graph. The project was built before AI coding assistants existed, so every part of the interface and the drawing logic had to be designed and written by hand.
contribution: Built the application in Java with JavaFX, with the help of a classmate, organised in a model, view and controller structure.
Matrix to graph: an editable matrix whose size can be increased or decreased, which generates the graph with one node per state and a directed, weighted arrow for every non-zero transition.
Graph to matrix: the user places and names the states, adds arrows with their probabilities, and the application produces the corresponding transition matrix.
Wrote a custom arrow component that draws a line with a correctly oriented arrowhead and keeps it attached to its nodes, since JavaFX has no built-in directed arrows.
Added input validation with clear error messages, for example when the probabilities leaving a state do not add up correctly or a state name is too long.
Designed the navigation between screens: home, matrix input, graph input and generated graph.
outcome: A working tool that turns a Markov chain from matrix to graph and back in a few clicks, with clean, readable graphs. Not a huge project, but a real challenge at the time: building interactive graph drawing by hand in JavaFX, without any AI help.

projects.title: Pharmacy manager
projects.summary: A desktop app to run a pharmacy: inventory, purchases and sales, and stock monitoring.

problem: A pharmacy has to know at every moment what it has in stock, what it bought and what it sold. Doing this on paper or in scattered spreadsheets leads to errors, products running out without warning, and no clear view of daily activity.
The goal was a desktop application that brings inventory, purchases, sales and stock monitoring together in one place.
stateOfArt: Professional pharmacy software exists, but it is complete, expensive and built for large organisations. Small pharmacies often fall back on spreadsheets, which do not prevent mistakes and do not update stock automatically when something is bought or sold.
contribution: Built the application on my own in Java with JavaFX.
Product inventory: adding and managing the products the pharmacy holds.
Purchases and sales: recording what comes in and what goes out, with the stock updated accordingly.
Stock monitoring, to follow quantities and see what is running low.
Stored all data in an SQL database, so the information is kept reliably between sessions.
outcome: A simple, working management application that keeps a pharmacy's inventory, purchases, sales and stock in one place. One of my first complete desktop applications, built in the final year of my bachelor's degree.
